title: TypeScript
blurb: Structural typing, narrowing, generics, and the boundary where types stop being guarantees. Nearly every JS role now screens on this.

questions.q: What is the difference between `any` and `unknown`?
choices: `any` disables checking entirely; `unknown` accepts anything but must be narrowed before use
`any` is a runtime type, `unknown` is compile-time
questions.why: `any` is contagious — every value derived from it is unchecked too. `unknown` is the safe top type: you can assign anything to it, but you cannot call, index or read it until you have proved what it is.
questions.asked: The clearest signal of whether someone uses TypeScript or just tolerates it.

questions.q: Does TypeScript exist at runtime?
choices: No — types are erased during compilation; nothing is checked when the code runs
Yes, types are checked at runtime
questions.why: This is why `typeof` and `instanceof` are the runtime tools, why you cannot `switch` on a type, and why data crossing the network boundary needs real validation rather than a type annotation.
questions.asked: Setting up the next question: how do you validate an API response?

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
questions.code: const user = await (await fetch('/api/me')).json() as User;
choices: `as` asserts without checking — if the API changed, this lies and crashes later
Nothing — this is the standard pattern
questions.why: json() returns `any`/`unknown`. `as User` just tells the compiler to stop asking; nothing verifies the shape. Validate at the boundary with a schema library or a hand-written type guard.
questions.asked: The single most valuable TypeScript question for a CRUD role.

questions.q: What does `satisfies` do that `as` does not?
choices: Checks the value against the type while keeping the narrower inferred type
It widens the type to the annotation
questions.why: `const config = {...} satisfies Config` errors if a key is wrong, but `config.mode` stays the literal `'dark'` rather than widening to `string`. An annotation would widen it; `as` would not check it at all.
questions.asked: A newer feature, so it signals whether someone keeps current.

questions.q: What is a discriminated union?
choices: A union of object types sharing a literal 'tag' field the compiler can narrow on
questions.why: `{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error'; error: Error } | { status: 'ok'; data: T }`. Checking `state.status === 'ok'` narrows the whole object, so `state.data` exists only where it can. It is the best tool in the language for CRUD UI state.
questions.asked: If you can describe this well you have effectively answered 'how do you model loading states?' too.

questions.q: How do you make a `switch` exhaustive?
choices: Assign the value to `never` in the default branch
questions.why: `default: { const _exhaustive: never = value; throw new Error(...) }`. When someone adds a new union member, that assignment stops compiling — the compiler tells you every place you forgot.
questions.asked: It demonstrates using the type system as a refactoring safety net, which is the real pitch for TypeScript.

questions.q: Is TypeScript structurally or nominally typed?
choices: Structurally — compatibility is decided by shape, not by declared name
Nominally — types must be declared to be related
Structurally for interfaces, nominally for classes
questions.why: Any object with the right properties satisfies an interface, even if it was never declared to implement it. That is why a `UserId` and an `OrderId` that are both `string` are interchangeable — and why branded types exist.

questions.q: What is a branded (nominal) type and why use one?
choices: A primitive intersected with a unique marker so distinct ids cannot be swapped
A type from a specific npm package
A class with a private field
A type alias with a comment
questions.why: `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }`. Now passing an OrderId where a UserId is expected fails to compile, even though both are strings at runtime. It costs one cast at the point of creation.
questions.asked: Comes up as 'how would you stop someone passing the wrong id?'

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `interface` and `type`?
choices: Interfaces can be merged by re-declaration and are used for object shapes; type aliases can express unions, tuples and mapped types
There is no difference at all
questions.why: Declaration merging matters when augmenting a library's types. Type aliases are the only way to write a union, a conditional type or a template literal type. For a plain object shape, either is fine — pick one and be consistent.
questions.asked: A guaranteed question. The bad answer is 'interfaces are for classes'.

questions.q: What does `strictNullChecks` change?
choices: null and undefined stop being assignable to every type, so they must be handled explicitly
questions.why: Without it, `string` silently includes null and the compiler cannot warn you. With it, you write `string | null` where absence is real and the compiler forces a check before use. It is the highest-value flag in the whole config.

questions.q: What is the difference between `foo?: string` and `foo: string | undefined`?
choices: The optional one may be omitted entirely; the union one must be present, possibly as undefined
The optional form allows null too
The union form is not valid TypeScript
questions.why: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes the distinction sharpens further. It matters for PATCH-style updates, where 'key absent' means 'leave alone' and 'key present but undefined' means 'clear it'.
questions.asked: A precise question that maps onto a real API design decision.

questions.q: What does this type resolve to?
questions.code:
type A = { id: number; name: string };
type B = Omit<A, 'name'> & { name: number };
questions.why: Omit removes `name` first, so the intersection adds it back with the new type rather than intersecting `string & number` (which would be never). This is the standard idiom for overriding one field of an existing type.

questions.q: What does `Partial<T>` do?
choices: Makes every property of T optional
Picks the first half of T's properties
questions.why: Useful for a PATCH payload or an options object. Its counterpart is Required<T>. Note Partial is shallow — nested objects keep their required fields.

questions.q: When is a generic actually needed?
choices: When a relationship between input and output types must be preserved
Whenever a function takes an object
questions.why: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` carries the element type through. A generic used once and never related to anything else is just `any` with extra syntax.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check whether generics are understood or cargo-culted.

questions.q: What does `keyof` produce?
questions.code: type Keys = keyof { id: number; name: string };
questions.why: A union of literal key types. Combined with a generic constraint it gives you a type-safe property getter: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.
questions.asked: The `get` function is one of the most common TypeScript live-coding exercises.

questions.q: What is wrong here?
choices: `map` does not exist on `string`, so the union must be narrowed first
string[] is not a valid type
Nothing — TypeScript infers the array case
questions.why: On a union you can only access members present on every branch. Narrow with `Array.isArray(input)` first — or normalise the input to an array at the top of the function.

questions.q: What is a user-defined type guard?
choices: A function returning `arg is Type`, which narrows the argument for the caller
questions.why: `function isUser(v: unknown): v is User { ... }`. The compiler trusts the signature, so the body has to actually check — a lazy guard is an `as` with more steps.

questions.q: What does `readonly` guarantee?
choices: Compile-time only — the property cannot be reassigned through that type, but nothing stops mutation at runtime
The object is frozen at runtime
questions.why: Types are erased. readonly and ReadonlyArray document and enforce intent during development; Object.freeze is the runtime tool, and it is shallow too.

questions.q: What does `as const` do?
choices: Infers the narrowest literal types and makes it deeply readonly — here `readonly ['home', 'about']`
Makes it a tuple of strings
questions.why: Without it the type is `string[]` and `routes[0]` is just `string`. With it you can derive a union: `type Route = typeof routes[number]`, which is `'home' | 'about'`.
questions.asked: A very practical trick — one source of truth for both a runtime list and a type.

questions.q: Should you use an `enum` or a union of string literals?
choices: Usually a union — it has no runtime output and is easier to serialise
Always an enum; unions are not type-safe
questions.why: A numeric enum emits a runtime object and its members accept any number in older versions. A string-literal union erases completely and matches the JSON you actually send. `const enum` has its own inlining caveats.
questions.asked: A good 'do you have an opinion' question; either answer is fine if you can justify it.

questions.q: What does this infer?
questions.code:
const config = { retries: 3, mode: 'dark' };
// typeof config.mode is?
questions.why: Mutable properties widen to their base type, since you could reassign them later. `as const`, or `satisfies` against a literal-typed field, keeps the literal.

questions.q: What is the `Result` pattern and why use it over throwing?
choices: Return `{ ok: true, value } | { ok: false, error }` so failure is visible in the type and must be handled
It is a library for retrying failed calls
It replaces try/catch entirely in all code
questions.why: A thrown error is invisible to the type system — nothing forces a caller to handle it. A Result makes the failure path part of the signature. The trade-off is verbosity, so most codebases use it for expected failures and throw for bugs.
questions.asked: A good design-opinion question, and it maps onto C#'s exceptions-vs-Result debate too.

questions.q: What does the `!` non-null assertion do?
choices: Tells the compiler the value is not null — with no runtime check, so it crashes if you are wrong
Throws a helpful error if null
Is required syntax for DOM access
questions.why: It is `as NonNullable<T>` in one character. Fine where you genuinely know more than the compiler, but an explicit `if (!el) throw new Error('#root is missing')` gives a real error message instead of 'cannot read property of null'.

questions.q: What does `Record<K, V>` express?
choices: An object type with keys K and values V
questions.why: `Record<'a' | 'b', number>` requires both keys — which is how you make a lookup table the compiler checks for completeness when the key union grows.

questions.q: Why can this be unsafe?
choices: Indexing gives `User` even when the key is missing, unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on
questions.why: By default TypeScript assumes any index into a Record or array succeeds. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to every index access and forces a check — noisier, but it catches real crashes.
questions.asked: A strong signal: it shows you have tuned a tsconfig rather than accepted the default.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` here?
choices: string in the first return, number in the second
questions.why: Control-flow analysis narrows inside the branch and — crucially — narrows the remainder by elimination after it. That is why an early return is often the cleanest way to narrow.

questions.q: What is the point of `never`?
choices: The type with no values — used for exhaustiveness checks and functions that never return
It means the same as void
It is the type of null
questions.why: `never` is assignable to everything and nothing is assignable to it, which is exactly what makes the exhaustive-switch trick work. A function that always throws is inferred as returning never.

questions.q: What is the difference between `void` and `undefined` as a return type?
choices: A `() => void` callback may return anything — the value is just ignored
undefined is not a valid return type
questions.why: This is deliberate: it lets `array.forEach(item => set.add(item))` typecheck even though add returns the Set. A return type of `undefined` would reject it.

questions.q: How should you type a function that takes an object and returns one of its values?
choices: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`
`function get(obj: Record<string, unknown>, key: string): unknown`
questions.why: The constraint ties the key to the object and the indexed access type ties the return to the key, so `get(user, 'name')` is `string` and `get(user, 'nope')` fails to compile.
questions.asked: The canonical 'write me a generic' exercise.

questions.q: What does `Pick<T, K>` do, and what is its opposite?
choices: Keeps only the listed keys; `Omit<T, K>` removes them
Selects the first K properties; `Drop` removes them
Extracts a union member; `Exclude` removes one
questions.why: Both are the standard way to derive a DTO from a domain model — e.g. `type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>`, so adding a sensitive field later cannot leak by accident.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile with strict mode on?
choices: It compiles — array assignment is covariant and unsound, so the push is allowed and breaks Dog[] at runtime
Dog does not extend Animal correctly
Arrays cannot be assigned across types
push is not available on Animal[]
questions.why: TypeScript deliberately allows covariant array assignment for ergonomics, which makes this unsound: you have just put a non-Dog into a Dog[]. Use ReadonlyArray for parameters you only read.
questions.asked: A deep-end question. Knowing the hole exists is worth more than being able to name 'covariance'.

questions.q: What is the safest way to handle a JSON payload of unknown shape?
choices: Type it as `unknown`, then validate with a schema or type guard that returns the typed value
Type it as `any` and access fields directly
Cast it with `as` to the expected interface
questions.why: Validation is the only thing that turns runtime data into a type you can trust. Libraries like Zod let one schema produce both the runtime check and the static type, so they cannot drift apart.
questions.asked: The practical heart of TypeScript in a CRUD app.

questions.q: What is 'make impossible states unrepresentable'?
choices: Modelling so that contradictory combinations cannot be constructed at all
questions.why: `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: Error }` permits loading-and-errored-and-loaded simultaneously. A discriminated union permits exactly three states, so half your defensive code disappears.
questions.asked: A phrase worth knowing — using it correctly signals real type-design experience.

questions.q: What does a `d.ts` file contain?
choices: Type declarations only, with no runtime code — used to describe JavaScript to TypeScript
questions.why: Ambient declarations. It is how `@types/*` packages describe untyped libraries, and how you declare globals or module augmentations in your own project.

questions.q: What does this template literal type produce?
questions.why: Template literal types distribute over unions and compose with the intrinsic string types (Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, Uncapitalize). Handy for deriving prop names or route params from a route string.

questions.q: Why might you prefer `unknown` in a catch clause?
choices: Anything can be thrown, so `error` is unknown by default under useUnknownInCatchVariables and must be narrowed
Because errors are always Error objects
questions.why: JavaScript lets you throw a string, a number, anything. Narrow with `error instanceof Error` before touching `.message`, and have a fallback for the rest.

questions.q: What does `Awaited<T>` do?
choices: Unwraps a promise type, recursively — `Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>>` is `string`
Waits for the type to resolve at runtime
Converts a callback type to a promise type
questions.why: Most useful with ReturnType: `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>` gives you the resolved data type without exporting it separately.

questions.q: Your build passes `tsc` but the app crashes in production on real data. What is the likely cause?
choices: An unvalidated boundary — the API returned a different shape than the type claimed
questions.why: The compiler only checks what it can see. Anything crossing a boundary — HTTP, localStorage, env vars, a JSON file, a message from a worker — is unchecked until you check it.
questions.asked: A scenario question that tests whether you understand the limits of the tool you use every day.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Extract<T, U>` and `Exclude<T, U>`?
choices: Extract keeps union members assignable to U; Exclude removes them
Extract works on objects, Exclude on unions
They are the same with reversed arguments
Extract pulls out a property type
questions.why: Both are conditional types distributing over a union. `Exclude<Status, 'archived'>` is how you derive a narrower state machine from a wider one without duplicating the list.

questions.q: Which tsconfig setting most improves safety for a new project?
choices: `"strict": true` — it turns on the whole family including strictNullChecks
questions.why: strict is an umbrella over strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes and more. Add noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes once the team is comfortable.
questions.asked: 'What's in your tsconfig?' is a quick way to gauge experience.
